$comment: What this study says about this animal. `record` names the homology group a row has been assigned to; null means nobody has assigned it yet, and `blockedBy` says what is missing. `status` mirrors data/remine-status.json: `scaffolded` means these rows came out of the old storage and NOBODY HAS CHECKED THEM AGAINST THE PAPER.

observations.name: Biceps brachii
observations.action: Flexes the forearm and supinates it; the long head assists flexion of the arm.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Long head from the supraglenoid tubercle, short head from the tip of the coracoid process, both to the radial tuberosity. **Both heads are coracoid heads in the outgroups** — in reptiles with two heads both arise from the coracoid, one tendinously and one fleshily, and only neognathous birds have evolved a humeral head. The human long head has migrated onto the scapula above the glenoid because the therian coracoid is reduced to a process of the scapula, so a change that looks like the muscle moving is the bone moving underneath it. Note also what is missing: the ulnar insertion present in lepidosaurs, reconstructed for *Tawa* and reported for some crocodylians is gone, leaving the radial tuberosity alone.

observations.name: Brachialis
observations.action: Flexes the forearm.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Anterior surface of the lower half of the humerus and the intermuscular septa, to the coronoid process of the ulna. Ulna only — the shared radius-and-ulna insertion of crocodylians and lepidosaurs, which Burch reconstructs for *Tawa*, has been restricted to the ulna in humans as it has independently in birds. Two clades arriving at the same restriction is the reason the *Tawa* row scores the plesiomorphic pattern on the absence of an anterior ulnar depression rather than on parsimony alone.

observations.name: Coracobrachialis
observations.action: Flexes and adducts the arm.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Coracoid process to the medial humerus at mid-shaft — a single belly where this record is a mass that carries two or three in the outgroups. The human muscle corresponds to the coracobrachialis medius; the brevis and longus of other tetrapods are not separately present. Its nerve is the reason it is worth reading beside the biceps and brachialis rows: all three are musculocutaneous, which is what identifies them as one ventral-mass series in the arm.

observations.name: Triceps brachii
observations.action: Extends the forearm; the long head extends and adducts the arm.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Three heads: long from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, lateral from the posterolateral humerus and lateral intermuscular septum, medial from the posteromedial surface of the lower half of the humerus, all onto the olecranon. **Three heads is not the ancestral count.** Crocodylians and lepidosaurs have four — scapular, coracoid, medial and lateral — and Burch reconstructs three in *Tawa* with the coracoid head already lost. Birds have lost the lateral head as well. The human long head is the scapular head; the coracoid head is gone with the coracoid, which is the same absence the subcoracoscapularis row records. The infraglenoid tubercle is scored as `scapula` without a landmark, since it is a named point on that bone rather than an element here.

observations.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). No caudal muscles are listed, and a human coccyx has essentially none of its own. **The musculature did not vanish, it changed job**: the iliococcygeus and coccygeus of the human pelvic floor are the iliocaudalis and ischiocaudalis of a tailed tetrapod, and they are scored on those records in `muscles-hindlimb.json`. A muscle group that moved a tail now holds the pelvic viscera in place.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed among the 16 muscles of the back region. A short dorsal rib muscle described for lepidosaurs; the human muscle nearest its position is the levatores costarum, which is scored on its own record and shares this one's dorsal-ramus supply.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. The ypsiloideus attaches to the ypsiloid cartilage, which is an anuran and urodele structure with no amniote counterpart, so the absence follows from the skeleton rather than from anything about the muscle.

observations.name: Abdominal wall, intercostal and subvertebral musculature
observations.action: Compresses the abdomen, flexes and rotates the trunk, and moves the ribs in respiration.
observations.innervation: Ventral primary rami of the spinal nerves throughout; the diaphragm by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5).
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). The whole ventral field, whose members have their own records and are scored there; quadratus lumborum is the subvertebral member and has none. **The diaphragm is scored as a disputed part and is the most interesting thing in this row.** It is a mammalian novelty with no counterpart in any other column here, and its nerve is the evidence for where it came from: the phrenic nerve arises from C3-C5, so the muscle is built from cervical hypaxial myotome that migrated caudally with its nerve trailing behind it. A nerve that long for a muscle that low is the record of the journey. Gest gives its origin as the xiphoid, the costal margin, the arcuate ligaments over quadratus lumborum and psoas major, and the bodies of L1-L3, all converging on a central tendon — a hypaxial sheet that ends on itself rather than on bone.

observations.name: Erector spinae and the transversospinal system
observations.action: Extends and laterally bends the trunk and neck; the suboccipital group extends and rotates the head on the atlas and axis.
observations.innervation: Dorsal primary rami of the spinal nerves, segmentally from C1 to S5.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **One field, segmentally supplied from the top of the neck to the sacrum, and every human name in it is a regional label rather than a muscle.** Gest lists erector spinae, iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis, semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores, interspinales, intertransversarii, splenius and the four suboccipital muscles, and gives all of them dorsal primary rami. That single fact is what makes the field one homology group: an epaxial muscle is defined by its nerve, not by its attachments, and this is the column where the definition is easiest to check. The three named tracts have their own records and are scored there.

observations.name: External abdominal oblique
observations.action: Compresses the abdomen; flexes and rotates the trunk.
observations.innervation: Intercostal nerves 7-11, subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lower eight ribs to the linea alba, pubic crest and tubercle, and the anterior half of the iliac crest, fibres running downward and forward. The outermost of the three sheets, and unchanged in principle from the arrangement in any tetrapod: three layers at three angles, all on ventral rami.

observations.name: External intercostal
observations.action: Elevates the ribs in inspiration.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lower border of a rib to the upper border of the rib below, fibres running downward and forward — the same direction as the external oblique, which is the continuation of this sheet into the abdomen. One layer, two names, divided by where the ribs stop.

observations.name: Iliocostalis
observations.action: Extends and laterally bends the trunk and neck.
observations.innervation: Dorsal primary rami of spinal nerves C4-S5.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Iliac crest and sacrum to the angles of the ribs — the lateral tract of the erector spinae, and the only one of the three that ends on ribs rather than on vertebrae. In a lizard the equivalent runs the length of the trunk without the lumbar interruption an upright posture imposes.

observations.name: Internal abdominal oblique
observations.action: Compresses the abdomen; flexes and rotates the trunk.
observations.innervation: Intercostal nerves 7-11, subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Thoracolumbar fascia, the anterior two-thirds of the iliac crest and the inguinal ligament, to the lower three or four ribs, the linea alba and the pubic crest — fibres running upward and forward, at right angles to the external oblique outside it. Gest also lists the cremaster, which is a slip of this sheet carried down onto the spermatic cord and has no counterpart in this dataset.

observations.name: Internal, innermost and subcostal intercostals
observations.action: Depresses the ribs in forced expiration.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Fibres running upward and forward, opposite to the external layer. Four named muscles here are one deep sheet interrupted by the neurovascular plane: internal and innermost intercostal are the two laminae either side of it, subcostalis is the same sheet spanning two or three ribs at the back, and transversus thoracis is the same sheet again on the inner surface of the sternum. Gest lists them separately because a dissector meets them separately.

observations.name: Levatores costarum
observations.action: Elevates the ribs.
observations.innervation: Dorsal primary rami of spinal nerves C7-T11.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Transverse processes of C7-T11 to the rib below, medial to its angle. **Dorsal rami, and that is the point**: this is a rib muscle that belongs to the epaxial field by nerve, which is what separates it from the intercostals lying just lateral to it on ventral rami. Gest's own table draws the line in the innervation column.

observations.name: Longissimus
observations.action: Extends and laterally bends the vertebral column; the capitis part extends the head.
observations.innervation: Dorsal primary rami of spinal nerves C1-S1.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Transverse process to transverse process, several levels up, and by the capitis division onto the mastoid process. The intermediate tract of the erector spinae, and the one that reaches furthest forward. The mastoid end was scored as `occiput` until 2026-08-20 because the skeleton carried no mastoid element; it does now, and the row was corrected rather than left approximating a petrosal attachment onto the occipital bone.

observations.name: Rectus abdominis
observations.action: Flexes the trunk; compresses the abdomen.
observations.innervation: Intercostal nerves 7-11 and the subcostal nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Pubis and pubic symphysis to the xiphoid process and costal cartilages 5-7. **The segmentation is visible.** The tendinous intersections that make the human 'six-pack' are the remnants of the myosepta that divide this muscle into serial blocks in a fish, and the segmental nerve supply Gest lists — seven separate nerves to one muscle — is the same fact stated in the innervation column. Pyramidalis is scored as a second part: a small triangular slip in front of the rectus, often absent, ending on the linea alba.

observations.name: Transversospinal system
observations.action: Extends and rotates the vertebral column; semispinalis capitis extends the head.
observations.innervation: Dorsal primary rami of spinal nerves C1-L5.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The deep layer, and the one whose subdivisions are defined by how far they reach.** Gest separates them exactly that way: rotatores span one or two vertebrae, multifidus two to four, semispinalis four to six, all running from a transverse process up and medially to a spinous process. Interspinales and intertransversarii are the shortest members, joining adjacent processes of the same kind. A single fibre orientation repeated at five different lengths, given five names.

observations.name: Transversus abdominis
observations.action: Compresses the abdomen.
observations.innervation: Intercostal nerves 7-11, subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lower six ribs, thoracolumbar fascia, the anterior three-quarters of the iliac crest and the inguinal ligament, to the linea alba and the pecten of the pubis, fibres running transversely. The innermost sheet; its fibres are the only ones of the three that run straight across.

observations.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. A urodele jaw opener that pulls against the hyobranchial apparatus rather than the skull; the human jaw is opened by the digastric, which pulls against the hyoid but is built from two arches and is scored on `depressor-mandibulae` and `intermandibularis`.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **Absent, and the reason to say so is that a human has a muscle of this name which is not this muscle.** The record holds the lepidosaur levator anguli oris, a trigeminal jaw muscle whose identification is the crux of the lizard-snake problem — in colubroid snakes the rictal plate becomes the venom gland and parts of the muscle insert onto the gland or the mandible. Gest's levator anguli oris is a facial-expression muscle on the facial nerve, running from the maxilla to the corner of the mouth, and is scored as part of the `interhyoideus` field. Two muscles, one name, two different cranial nerves and two different arches.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. The spiracular series has no muscle in a human — but the region does survive: the spiracular pouch is the ancestor of the tympanic cavity, so the space this muscle worked in became the middle ear. The two muscles a human does have in that cavity, tensor tympani and stapedius, come from the mandibular and hyoid arches respectively and are scored on `intermandibularis` and `stapedius`.

observations.name: Extraocular muscles and levator palpebrae superioris

parts.name: Superior, inferior, medial and lateral rectus

observations.action: Rotate the eyeball about three axes; levator palpebrae raises the upper eyelid.
observations.innervation: Oculomotor nerve (III), except superior oblique (trochlear, IV) and lateral rectus (abducens, VI).
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Four recti and two obliques from the common tendinous ring and the orbital wall onto the sclera. **The three-nerve pattern is the most conserved arrangement in the vertebrate head** — one muscle to the trochlear nerve, one to the abducens, the rest to the oculomotor — and it is identical in a lamprey, a shark and a human, which is why this record's development field reads prechordal/somitomeric rather than branchiomeric. What a human lacks is the retractor bulbi, present in most tetrapods on the abducens; levator palpebrae superioris is scored as a fourth part and is the addition going the other way.

observations.name: Facial expression musculature and platysma
observations.action: Move the skin of the face, scalp, eyelids and lips; close the eye and the mouth; compress the cheek against the teeth.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The single largest expansion of any muscle group in this dataset.** The ancestral interhyoideus is one ventral sheet of the hyoid arch, a constrictor; in a human it has spread over the whole head as some thirty named muscles, and Gest's head and neck table is mostly them. Almost none of them reaches bone at both ends: they arise from the skull and insert into skin, which is what a sphincter sheet does when it stops encircling something. Every one of them is on the facial nerve, which is the only reason they can be recognised as one group at all — the same criterion this dataset uses for the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid, and for the four trigeminal muscles of the `intermandibularis` row. The listed parts are the principal members, not the full set.

observations.name: Infrahyoid, suprahyoid and tongue musculature
observations.action: Depress and fix the hyoid and larynx; protrude, retract and change the shape of the tongue.
observations.innervation: Hypoglossal nerve (XII) to the tongue and geniohyoid; ansa cervicalis to the infrahyoid strap muscles; palatoglossus by the vagus (X).
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **A muscle group that walked forward from the shoulder into the mouth, and its nerve is the receipt.** These are trunk muscles: hypobranchial myotome that migrated under the pharynx carrying the hypoglossal nerve and the ansa cervicalis with it, which is why the tongue of a human is supplied by a nerve that leaves the skull and comes back. Gest's list preserves the whole gradient — sternohyoid and omohyoid still reach the sternum and the scapula, geniohyoid stops at the mandible, and the intrinsic tongue muscles have no bony attachment at all. Palatoglossus is scored as a disputed part: it is in the tongue and named with the tongue muscles, but it takes the vagus and belongs with the palatal muscles on `branchial-constrictors`.

observations.name: Masseter, temporalis, the pterygoids and the tensors
observations.action: Elevate the mandible; the lateral pterygoid protracts it and opens the jaw; the pterygoids together produce lateral grinding.
observations.innervation: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Masseter from the zygomatic arch, temporalis from the temporal fossa, medial and lateral pterygoid from the pterygoid plates and the maxillary tuberosity, all to the mandible. **Four muscles, one nerve, and the nerve is the whole argument.** This record calls trigeminal innervation invariant and the muscle present wherever jaws are — the single most robust cranial homology in Gnathostomata. It also warns that subdivision patterns carry no homology weight on their own and the named parts are frequently non-homologous between clades, which is why the four human muscles are scored as parts of this record and **not** distributed among the `adductor-mandibulae-externus`, `-internus`, `-longus`, `-lateralis` and `-posterior` records. Those carve the sauropsid and anuran complex following Johnston's folded-sheet model, which is not a scheme a human jaw can be fitted into without inventing the fit.
observations.divisionNote: The tensors are here on Diogo et al. (2008) Table 1, which derives the tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini from the adductor mandibulae A2-PVM bundle and places them on the adductor row for all five mammals it examines — matching the *Ornithorhynchus* and *Rattus* rows on this record. Gest's tables put both on the mylohyoid instead, which is why they stay `membership: "disputed"` with the other claimant named.

observations.name: Mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric
observations.action: Elevates the floor of the mouth and the hyoid; tensor tympani damps the ossicular chain; tensor veli palatini tenses the soft palate and opens the auditory tube.
observations.innervation: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **This record's own assessment says the mammalian derivatives illustrate the point better than any limb example, and this is that row**: a muscle that ends up inside the ear still carries CN V. Mylohyoid keeps the ancestral sheet between the two mandibular rami, meeting its fellow at a midline raphe; the anterior belly of digastric is a strap cut out of the same sheet; tensor veli palatini has moved back into the palate; and tensor tympani has left the mouth altogether to insert on the malleus, scored here as `hyomandibula-stapes`, the middle-ear element group. Four muscles in four unrelated places, one trigeminal nerve, one ancestral sheet.
observations.divisionNote: The tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini were parts of this row until Diogo et al. (2008) Table 1 was read against it. They derive both from the adductor mandibulae A2-PVM bundle they identify in *Latimeria*, *Ambystoma* and *Timon*, and place them on their adductor row for all five mammals they examine. **Gest's tables, which put them here, describe one animal and settle no homology across taxa**, so under the rule in `docs/METHODS.md` the newer comparative treatment governs and the two muscles now sit on `adductor-mandibulae`. Nothing about arch identity turns on it — both fields are mandibular-arch and both take CN V — but a student now finds the muscle in one place instead of two.

observations.name: Pharyngeal constrictors, the palatal and laryngeal muscles
observations.action: Constrict the pharynx in swallowing; elevate the larynx and pharynx; tense, abduct and adduct the vocal folds.
observations.innervation: Vagus (X) through the pharyngeal plexus and the recurrent laryngeal nerve; stylopharyngeus by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The branchial arches after the gills are gone.** Three constrictors wrapping the pharynx onto a midline raphe are the arch constrictors of a fish doing the same job on a different tube; the intrinsic laryngeal muscles are the same series again, reduced to moving three small cartilages. The nerve split is the evidence and Gest records it: stylopharyngeus alone takes the glossopharyngeal nerve, arch three, while everything else takes the vagus, arches four and beyond — so one muscle in the middle of a topologically continuous sheet carries a different cranial nerve because it belongs to a different arch. Cricothyroid takes the external laryngeal branch and the rest take the recurrent laryngeal, which is the second such line drawn inside the same group. **Diogo et al. (2008) find that only one true branchial muscle survives in a human**, and it is the stylopharyngeus — see this record's homology notes and the lizard, platypus and rat rows below.

observations.name: Posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid
observations.action: Elevates the hyoid; with the anterior belly, depresses the mandible.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Posterior belly from the mastoid notch, stylohyoid from the styloid process, both onto the hyoid. **The digastric is two muscles from two arches sharing one tendon**: the anterior belly is trigeminal and is scored on `intermandibularis`, the posterior belly is facial and is scored here. A human jaw opener made by splicing a mandibular-arch muscle to a hyoid-arch one, which no non-mammal does. In other tetrapods this record's muscle runs straight from the skull to the retroarticular process and opens the jaw by itself.

observations.name: Stapedius
observations.action: Damps movement of the stapes.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). From a pyramidal eminence in the middle-ear wall to the neck of the stapes — **the smallest skeletal muscle in the human body, and one of the most important rows in this dataset for arch identity.** It is the depressor hyomandibulae of a shark, on the same facial nerve, still attached to the same element: this project keeps the hyomandibula and the stapes as one skeletal record precisely so that the shark's muscle and this one do not appear to attach to different bones. Its partner in the ear, tensor tympani, is trigeminal and belongs to the mandibular arch, so the two ossicular muscles are from two different arches and their nerves say so.

observations.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed, as in the hand. The one contrahens the human foot retains is the adductor hallucis, scored on [[contrahentes-digitorum-pes]]; the long head of the contrahens layer is gone from both limbs.
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. Only the lateral member of the pair survives in a human foot, as the quadratus plantae; see [[flexor-accessorius-lateralis-pes]].

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). As in the hand, the human interossei of the foot are scored once — on [[flexores-breves-profundi-pes]] — and the claim this record has on them is recorded rather than acted on. Howell (1936) found the relationship between Interossei, Intermetacarpales, Dorsometacarpales and Contrahentes digitorum unclear across tetrapods, and nothing in a human table resolves it.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). The human dorsal interossei of the foot are scored once, on [[flexores-breves-profundi-pes]], whose mammalian synonymy names them. This record exists because Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) separate a dorsal interosseous series from the short digital extensors in sauropsids — a distinction drawn on archosaur and lepidosaur material, not on mammals — so whether the human muscles belong here as well is not something Gest's table can settle. Uncertain rather than a second copy of the same observation.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. The human leg has no pronator: the tibia and fibula do not rotate on each other the way the radius and ulna do, and the interosseous membrane between them is a strut rather than an axis. Compare the forearm, where three separate pronators and a supinator are scored.

observations.name: Abductor digiti minimi
observations.action: Abducts the fifth digit.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medial and lateral sides of the calcaneal tuberosity to the lateral base of the proximal phalanx of digit V — the postaxial marginal muscle, the mirror of the abductor hallucis across the sole. In the hand the equivalent muscle arises from the pisiform, a sesamoid the foot has no counterpart for, so the two limbs reach the same arrangement from different bones.

observations.name: Abductor hallucis
observations.action: Abducts and flexes the great toe.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medial side of the calcaneal tuberosity to the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the hallux — the preaxial marginal muscle of the sole, in the position its forelimb counterpart the abductor pollicis brevis occupies in the palm.

observations.name: Adductor hallucis
observations.action: Adducts the great toe.
observations.innervation: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Oblique head from the bases of metatarsals 2-4, transverse head from the heads of metatarsals 3-5, both to the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the hallux. **The foot and the hand each kept exactly one contrahens, and it is the one to digit I in both.** Adductor hallucis here, adductor pollicis on `contrahentes-digitorum` — two limbs, the same survivor, the same two-headed arrangement, in an animal that uses the two limbs for completely different things.

observations.name: Extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis
observations.action: Extend the metatarsophalangeal joints of digits 1-4.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Both from the superolateral surface of the calcaneus; brevis to the extensor expansions of toes 1-4, hallucis brevis to the dorsum of the proximal phalanx of the hallux. **The hand lost this layer and the foot kept it** — see the `extensores-digitorum-breves` row, scored absent for the human hand. Both limbs of one animal, one retaining the ancestral short extensor sheet and the other not, which is a caution against reading the two limbs as versions of each other.

observations.name: Flexor digitorum brevis
observations.action: Flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints of digits 2-5.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Calcaneal tuberosity, plantar aponeurosis and intermuscular septa, to the bases of the middle phalanges of digits 2-5, splitting to let the long flexor tendons through. **The split tendon is inherited, not invented.** The same bifurcation is described for crocodylians, lepidosaurs and turtles in the hand, where the short flexor tendons divide to pass the long flexor, and Burch reconstructs it for *Tawa*. Humans kept it in the foot and lost the layer in the hand — see the `flexores-breves-superficiales` row, scored uncertain there for exactly that reason.

observations.name: Interossei and the short flexors of the hallux and fifth digit
observations.action: Flex the metatarsophalangeal joints; the interossei abduct and adduct the digits about the axis of digit II.
observations.innervation: Lateral plantar nerve, deep branch; flexor hallucis brevis by the medial plantar nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Four dorsal interossei from adjacent metatarsal shafts, three plantar interossei from the bases and medial sides of metatarsals 3-5, flexor hallucis brevis from the cuboid and lateral cuneiform, flexor digiti minimi brevis from the base of metatarsal V. **Scored on this record's own mammalian synonymy**, which names the interossei plantares and dorsales as its mammalian representatives. The same carve-up is contested in the hand and is handled the same way there. Note the axis: the human hand abducts about digit III and the foot about digit II, so the two sets of interossei are arranged around different rays.

observations.name: Quadratus plantae
observations.action: Redirects the pull of the long digital flexor along the axis of the foot.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Anterior calcaneus and the long plantar ligament, inserting not on bone but on the flexor digitorum longus tendons. **The hand lost this muscle and the foot kept it**, which is the opposite of the digital-extensor case and the reverse of what a strict serial reading of the two limbs would predict. Its job is purely mechanical: the long flexor enters the sole obliquely from the medial side, and this muscle pulls its tendons straight before they reach the toes.

observations.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. The ulnocarpalis is present in urodeles and monotremes and gone in a human hand; Gambaryan et al. (2015) argue it survives in *Ornithorhynchus* against the transverse subcarpal ligament, and Straus (1942) reported that ligament in some lipotyphlan insectivores. Neither muscle nor ligament is in a human, which is why this record's therian rows are thin.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed among the 54 upper limb muscles, and scored absent on that basis. **The interest is what it leaves behind**: this muscle bridges the medial epicondyle to the olecranon, and in a human that span is occupied by the cubital tunnel retinaculum, over the ulnar nerve — the same nerve the muscle carries wherever it is present. The record's own consensus action already says the muscle 'forms part of the cubital tunnel roof over the ulnar nerve'. Present in turtles, lepidosaurs, galloanseriform birds, *Apteryx* and tinamous, reconstructed for *Tawa* at 0.863, and repeatedly absorbed into flexor carpi ulnaris where it survives.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed for the hand. **The foot kept it**: the human quadratus plantae is the surviving flexor accessorius of the pes, and is scored on `flexor-accessorius-lateralis-pes`. A muscle present in one limb and absent in the serially corresponding position of the other, in the same animal — which is a caution about serial correspondence rather than evidence for it.
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed; see [[flexor-accessorius-lateralis]] for the hand-versus-foot contrast.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed, and absent in mammals generally. Its distribution is one of the odder ones on this dataset: absent in crocodylians, *Sphenodon* and paleognaths except tinamous, present in squamates, turtles and every neognath studied, which is enough for Burch (2014) to reconstruct it as unequivocally present in theropods despite one bracketing clade lacking it entirely. Mammals are simply outside that distribution.

observations.name: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
observations.action: Abducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint; extensor pollicis brevis extends it at the metacarpophalangeal joint.
observations.innervation: Deep branch of the radial nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Abductor pollicis longus from the middle third of the posterior radius, the interosseous membrane and the mid-posterolateral ulna, to the radial side of the base of the first metacarpal; extensor pollicis brevis from the membrane and the distal posterior radius to the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. **Both bones is the archosaur condition too** — Burch (2014) makes the two-headed origin from the facing surfaces of radius and ulna a synapomorphy of Archosauria at 0.955, against a purely ulnar origin in lepidosaurs and turtles, so humans and birds share a bipennate origin that is not shared by descent. Extensor pollicis brevis is scored as the second part of the group on this record's own synonymy, which names the muscle 'abductor et extensor digiti I'.

observations.name: Anconeus
observations.action: Extends the forearm.
observations.innervation: Nerve to anconeus, from the radial nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lateral epicondyle to the lateral olecranon and the upper quarter of the ulna. Gest gives it its own named branch of the radial nerve, which is the observation that keeps it separate from the triceps in a human — this record's assessment is that the anconeus separates from and refuses to the triceps field readily, varying at species level inside every major clade. The insertion is much shorter than in the outgroups: Burch reconstructs it running most of the length of the ulna in *Tawa* at a probability near 1.0, and here it stops at the proximal quarter.

observations.name: Brachioradialis
observations.action: Flexes the elbow; assists pronation and supination toward mid-position.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Upper two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge to the lateral side of the base of the radial styloid process — scored as `radius[distal]`, since the styloid process in this skeleton is the cranial one. **A muscle of the extensor compartment, on the extensor nerve, that flexes the elbow**, which is why this record's confidence is only moderate: it is present in turtles, crocodylians, *Sphenodon* and mammals and absent or uncertain in amphibians, most lepidosaurs and birds, and whether that is one ancestral muscle repeatedly lost or repeated differentiation out of the radial extensor mass is unresolved. Burch's (2014) theropod 'supinator' is scored on this record — read the *Tawa* row beside this one, because the two carry different names for what the synonymy says is the same muscle.

observations.name: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
observations.action: Extends the wrist and abducts the hand.
observations.innervation: Radial nerve (longus); deep branch of the radial nerve (brevis).
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Longus from the lower third of the lateral supracondylar ridge to the base of the second metacarpal; brevis from the common extensor tendon on the lateral epicondyle to the base of the third. **This is the distal insertion shift the record is built around.** Turtles, lepidosaurs and crocodylians stop at the radius and proximal carpals; mammals and some grasping tree frogs have carried the insertion out onto the metacarpals independently, and Abdala & Diogo tie that shift to fine digital control. The human row is the mammalian end of a convergence, not evidence of a shared derived state.

observations.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
observations.action: Extends the wrist and adducts the hand.
observations.innervation: Deep branch of the radial nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Common extensor tendon and the middle half of the posterior border of the ulna, to the medial side of the base of the fifth metacarpal — insertion on the lateralmost metacarpal, which Burch (2014) argues is the plesiomorphic archosaur state too. **The name is a hazard on this record and the human row is the least confusing instance of it**: Meers calls the crocodylian muscle flexor ulnaris, Burch reassigns that name to the anconeus and codes extensor carpi ulnaris absent in crocodylians altogether. In a human it is an extensor by mass, by nerve and by action, with nothing arguing otherwise.

observations.name: Extensor digitorum and extensor digiti minimi
observations.action: Extends the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints of digits 2-5; extends the wrist.
observations.innervation: Deep branch of the radial nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Both from the common extensor tendon on the lateral epicondyle; extensor digiti minimi joins the extensor digitorum tendon to the fifth digit rather than reaching bone on its own. **The insertion is not on a phalanx at all** — it is the extensor expansion, the fibrous hood over the dorsum of each digit that the intrinsic muscles also insert into, so the long extensor and the lumbricals and interossei act on the interphalangeal joints through one shared structure. In the outgroups this muscle ends on the bases of the metacarpals or on the terminal phalanges directly. The expansion is what replaces those attachments.

observations.name: Extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis
observations.action: Extends the thumb at the interphalangeal joint and the index finger at all three joints.
observations.innervation: Deep branch of the radial nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Extensor pollicis longus from the interosseous membrane and the middle posterolateral ulna to the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb; extensor indicis from the membrane and the distal ulna, joining the extensor digitorum tendon to digit II. **These are the two muscles Diogo & Abdala use to define this record**, which exists to hold the deep dorsal antebrachial layer that turtles and lepidosaurs also have and that the superficial extensor digitorum obscures. The third member of their set, extensor digiti III proprius, is not present in a human.

observations.name: Flexor carpi radialis
observations.action: Flexes the wrist and abducts the hand.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Common flexor tendon to the bases of the second and third metacarpals — the flexor mirror of the extensor carpi radialis rows, reaching the same two bones from the other side of the hand. Note the naming trap this record carries: Sullivan, Dilkes and others call the avian muscle in this position 'pronator superficialis', while Burch's Table 1 gives that same avian name to the pronator teres. The human column is where the two are unambiguously separate muscles with separate nerves.

observations.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
observations.action: Flexes the wrist and adducts the hand.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Common flexor tendon and an ulnar head from the medial olecranon and the upper two-thirds of the posterior ulna, inserting on the pisiform, the hook of the hamate and the base of the fifth metacarpal. **The pisiform insertion is the plesiomorphic one and humans still have it**, which is not true of either extant archosaur clade: birds lost the pisiform and relocated the muscle to a neomorphic 'pseudoulnare' that is not the tetrapod ulnare at all. The hamate and metacarpal attachments are scored as `distal-carpals` and `metacarpals` rather than as new elements, on the rule that an element here is a homology group and not one species' bone name.

observations.name: Flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus
observations.action: Superficialis flexes the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints; profundus also flexes the distal interphalangeal joints.
observations.innervation: Median nerve; the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus is supplied by the ulnar nerve.
observations.attachmentNote:
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The two-layer arrangement this record exists to explain, in the animal it is named from.** Superficialis from the common flexor tendon and the middle third of the radius to the shafts of the middle phalanges of digits 2-5; profundus from the ulna and interosseous membrane to the bases of the distal phalanges; and the two insert at different levels on the same digits, the superficialis tendon splitting to let the profundus tendon through. That split-level insertion is the mammalian novelty. In amphibians and reptiles this is a single plate whose tendons end on the terminal phalanges, which is what Burch reconstructs for *Tawa*.

Flexor pollicis longus is scored as a third part: it is the deep flexor to digit I, separated off. **The divided nerve supply is the detail worth keeping** — Gest gives the radial half of profundus to the median nerve and the ulnar half to the ulnar nerve, so one muscle belly spans the boundary between two nerves of the same ventral division.

observations.name: Palmaris longus
observations.action: Tenses the palmar aponeurosis; weak wrist flexion.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Common flexor tendon to the palmar aponeurosis. **This record is quoted because its deep homology is not established, and the human muscle is the referent, not the evidence.** Abdala & Diogo name the 'palmaris longus' and the 'rhomboideus' as the two structures whose correspondence with the mammalian muscles of those names is explicitly under-supported, and ask for innervation and development across a broader amphibian and reptilian sample. Burch's (2014) Table 1 answers from a fourth direction, equating Walker's chelonian 'palmaris longus' with the humeral head of flexor digitorum longus instead. Gest also lists a palmaris brevis, a dermal muscle of the hypothenar skin with no counterpart anywhere else in this dataset; it is not scored.

observations.name: Pronator quadratus
observations.action: Pronates the forearm.
observations.innervation: Anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medial side of the anterior surface of the distal quarter of the ulna to the anterior surface of the distal quarter of the radius. **Distally restricted, like a bird's and unlike a lizard's.** Crocodylians, lepidosaurs and most turtles take the origin from more than half the length of the ulna; birds restrict it to the distal half or less, and so does a human. The carpal insertion present in turtles and some lepidosaurs, reconstructed for *Tawa* at 0.783 and surviving in birds as an attachment to the carpometacarpus, is gone here — the human muscle reaches the radius and stops.

observations.name: Pronator teres
observations.action: Pronates the forearm and assists elbow flexion.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Common flexor tendon and a deep ulnar head from the medial coronoid process, to the midpoint of the lateral radial shaft. **The insertion has contracted to a point.** In turtles, most lepidosaurs, crocodylians, paleognaths and the reconstruction for *Tawa* it is an elongate strip running more than half the length of the radius, at 0.815 at both the Aves and Archosauria nodes; the human muscle inserts at mid-shaft only. The two-headed origin is shared with the outgroups; the restricted insertion is not.

observations.name: Supinator
observations.action: Supinates the forearm, independently of elbow position.
observations.innervation: Deep branch of the radial nerve, which pierces the muscle and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lateral epicondyle, the supinator crest and fossa of the ulna, and the radial collateral and annular ligaments, to the lateral side of the proximal third of the radius. **This is the only column on this record that is not an argument about a name.** The word 'supinator' is applied by different authors to at least three non-homologous muscles — the crocodylian brachioradialis, part of the avian extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis, and the abductor pollicis longus as 'supinator manus'. The therian supinator, this muscle, has no confidently identified counterpart outside Mammalia, and the human row is what the other three are being mistaken for.

observations.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). As for [[intermetacarpales]]: the human interossei are scored once, on [[flexores-breves-profundi]], and this record's claim on them is recorded rather than acted on. Burch's *Tawa* row here is uncertain for a different reason — the muscles are almost certainly present but leave no osteological correlate to reconstruct from.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **Absent, and the absence is worth a row.** Gest lists 54 muscles of the upper limb and no short dorsal digital extensor among them; the human hand has no extensor digitorum brevis manus as a normal structure, though it is a recognised variant. Every other amniote column on this record has one. The foot kept its equivalent — see `extensores-digitorum-breves-pes`, where the human extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis are scored — so this is a loss in the hand specifically, in the limb that became a manipulator.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Scored uncertain rather than absent, and the uncertainty is about which record the human muscles belong to, not about what is there. The superficial short flexor layer has no muscle in the human hand that is unambiguously its own: the candidates — palmaris brevis, the superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis — are assigned to this layer by some authors and to the deep layer by others, and the deep layer's members are scored on `flexores-breves-profundi`. Compare the foot, where flexor digitorum brevis is the surviving superficial layer and is scored plainly. The hand lost the layer or absorbed it; the sources do not agree which.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). The human dorsal and palmar interossei are scored on [[flexores-breves-profundi]], whose synonymy already claims them. This record's synonymy claims them too — 'part of interossei dorsales' — and Howell (1936) found the relationship between Interossei, Intermetacarpales, Dorsometacarpales and Contrahentes digitorum unclear across tetrapods generally. Scored uncertain rather than duplicating the attachment rows onto a second record, which would give one observation two homes.

observations.name: Abductor digiti minimi
observations.action: Abducts the fifth digit.
observations.innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Pisiform to the ulnar side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the fifth digit — the same origin crocodylians, lizards and turtles use, and the same phalangeal insertion lepidosaurs and turtles use rather than the crocodylian metacarpal one. **The pisiform is what makes this row possible**, and it is the bone birds lost: Burch found the muscle in *Struthio* only because it had relocated to the neomorphic pseudoulnare, which was the first report of it in an avian manus. A human keeps the plesiomorphic arrangement intact.

observations.name: Abductor pollicis brevis
observations.action: Abducts the thumb.
observations.innervation: Recurrent branch of the median nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Flexor retinaculum, scaphoid and trapezium, to the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. The distal insertion — on the phalanx rather than on metacarpal I — is the state found in turtles, most lepidosaurs and all birds, and reconstructed for *Tawa* at 0.837; crocodylians, *Sphenodon* and *Liolaemus* keep the more proximal metacarpal insertion. **The origin is the variable end** across every clade this record holds, and the human version adds a retinaculum the outgroups do not have. Scaphoid and trapezium are scored as `carpals` and `distal-carpals`; naming them as elements would create two bones for one species.

observations.name: Adductor pollicis
observations.action: Adducts the thumb.
observations.innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Oblique head from the capitate and the bases of the second and third metacarpals, transverse head from the shaft of the third, both to the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. **One contrahens survives in a human and this is it.** The contrahens layer runs a muscle to every digit in a lizard or a crocodylian; humans have lost all of them except the one to digit I, which is why the adductor pollicis has no partner and looks like a thenar muscle rather than a member of a series. Compare the *Tawa* row on this record, scored uncertain because Burch expects the same layer to have been lost there for the same kind of reason — reduction of the lateral digits.

observations.name: Interossei and the deep thenar and hypothenar muscles
observations.action: Flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints; the interossei abduct and adduct the digits about the axis of digit III; the opponens muscles rotate the first and fifth metacarpals.
observations.innervation: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve, except the thenar muscles, which take the recurrent branch of the median nerve.
observations.attachmentNote:
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **A large and openly contested carve-up, scored here on this record's own synonymy**, which already equates the deep short flexor layer with the mammalian interossei. Four dorsal interossei each from two adjacent metacarpal shafts; four palmar interossei from the palmar shafts of metacarpals 1, 2, 4 and 5; and the thenar and hypothenar short flexors and opponens muscles from the flexor retinaculum and the distal carpals. All insert on the proximal phalanges and, for the interossei, into the extensor expansion as well.

**The alternative assignments are real and are not settled here.** McMurrich, Howell and Lewis do not agree on how Interossei, Intermetacarpales, Dorsometacarpales and Contrahentes digitorum divide up, and Howell (1936) said as much. `intermetacarpales` and `dorsometacarpales` in this dataset both carry 'part of interossei dorsales' in their synonymy, so the human interossei have a claim on those two records as well; the rows there are scored uncertain and point back here rather than duplicating this one. The first palmar interosseus is often fused to the adductor pollicis, which is scored on `contrahentes-digitorum` — so the boundary between two of these records is, in a human, sometimes not a boundary.

observations.name: Lumbricals
observations.action: Flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints of digits 2-5.
observations.innervation: Median nerve to the radial two; deep branch of the ulnar nerve to the ulnar two.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). From the flexor digitorum profundus tendons of digits 2-5 to the extensor expansion on the radial side of each proximal phalanx. **A muscle with no bony attachment at either end**, running from one tendon to another — which is why the *Tawa* row on this record carries no attachments at all: Burch judges the reconstruction too speculative because number and insertion vary so much, and there are no osteological correlates for a muscle that never touches bone. The human split nerve supply, median to the radial two and ulnar to the ulnar two, is the same boundary that divides flexor digitorum profundus.

observations.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed, and the structure in its position is the interosseous membrane — a ligament where a salamander has a muscle. It is not simply lost: the popliteus derives from it, and is scored on that record. One ancestral muscle here becomes a ligament and a knee rotator in the same animal.

observations.name: Extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus
observations.action: Extend the toes and dorsiflex the foot.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Extensor digitorum longus from the lateral tibial condyle, the anterior fibula and the interosseous membrane to the extensor expansions of the lateral four toes; extensor hallucis longus from the middle fibula to the distal phalanx of the hallux. **Fibularis tertius is scored here as a disputed part rather than with the fibularis group**, and the reason is its nerve: Diogo & Molnar make the point that fibularis tertius and fibularis digiti quinti are supplied by the DEEP fibular nerve, with the extensors, not by the superficial fibular nerve that supplies the true fibularis muscles. The name groups it with the peronei; the innervation groups it here.

observations.name: Fibularis longus and brevis
observations.action: Evert the foot and assist plantarflexion.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Longus from the upper two-thirds of the lateral fibula, crossing the sole deep to the intrinsic muscles to reach the medial cuneiform and the first metatarsal; brevis from the lower third to the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal. **Only the two superficial-fibular muscles are scored on this record.** Fibularis tertius carries the group's name and the extensors' nerve, and is scored with `extensor-digitorum-longus-hl` instead — this record's assessment already says the innervation cuts against the obvious grouping, and this is what acting on that looks like. Note also the longus tendon: it crosses the whole sole transversely, so a lateral muscle ends on the medial side of the foot.

observations.name: Flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus
observations.action: Flex the toes and assist plantarflexion of the foot.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Flexor digitorum longus from the middle half of the posterior tibia to the distal phalanges of digits 2-5; flexor hallucis longus from the lower two-thirds of the posterior fibula to the distal phalanx of the hallux. **The hand and the foot went opposite ways here.** In the hand the long flexor split into a superficial and a deep layer inserting at two levels on the same digits; in the foot it split by digit instead, one muscle for the hallux and one for the rest, both reaching the terminal phalanges as the ancestral single plate did. Compare the `flexor-digitorum-longus` human row.

observations.name: Popliteus
observations.action: Unlocks the extended knee by laterally rotating the femur on the tibia.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lateral femoral condyle to the posterior tibia above the soleal line. **A muscle that has moved to the other end of a bone.** Its ancestor is the interosseus cruris, a muscle running between tibia and fibula in the position an amniote fills with the interosseous membrane; the popliteus has left the fibula and climbed onto the femur, converting a leg muscle into a knee muscle. That is why `interosseus-cruris` is scored absent in a human on the next record and this one is present.

observations.name: Tibialis anterior
observations.action: Dorsiflexes and inverts the foot.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lateral tibial condyle and the upper lateral tibial surface to the medial cuneiform and the first metatarsal — the preaxial dorsiflexor, unchanged in position from the amphibian extensor cruris tibialis and reaching the same first-digit side of the foot. The medial cuneiform is scored as `distal-tarsals`.

observations.name: Tibialis posterior
observations.action: Inverts the foot and assists plantarflexion.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Interosseous membrane and the facing surfaces of both leg bones, to the navicular tuberosity, the medial cuneiform and metatarsals 2-4 — the widest tarsal insertion of any muscle in the human foot, and the main dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch.

observations.name: Triceps surae and plantaris
observations.action: Plantarflexes the foot; gastrocnemius also flexes the knee.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Gastrocnemius from above the two femoral condyles, soleus from the fibular head and the soleal line of the tibia, plantaris from above the lateral condyle, all to the dorsum of the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon. **Femoral and tibial origins at once**, which is what this record says varies: head count and the femoral-versus-tibial origin are the two variables across Tetrapoda, and a human has both states in one muscle group. In anurans the same muscle is the principal jump-propulsion muscle and is hypertrophied past everything else in the leg.

observations.name: Deltoid, pars acromialis and pars spinata
observations.action: Abducts the arm; the posterior fibres extend and laterally rotate it.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). The acromial and spinous parts of a deltoid that is undivided at dissection; see the deltoideus clavicularis row, which carries the other part of the same human muscle and the reason for splitting it. Insertion on the deltoid tuberosity — the deltopectoral crest under its human name, and the same site the clavicular part uses.

observations.name: Deltoid, pars clavicularis
observations.action: Flexes and medially rotates the arm; assists abduction.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The human deltoid is one muscle in dissection and two records here**, and the split is not arbitrary: the clavicular part is the procoracohumeralis/deltoideus clavicularis of the outgroups and the acromial and spinous parts are the deltoideus scapularis, so a single human belly spans two homology groups that are separate muscles in a lizard. Gest gives the whole muscle one origin line — lateral third of the clavicle, acromion, lower lip of the crest of the scapular spine — and one insertion, the deltoid tuberosity, which is the human name for the deltopectoral crest. Both halves therefore carry the same insertion row, which is the honest representation of a fused insertion rather than a duplication.

observations.name: Latissimus dorsi
observations.action: Extends and medially rotates the arm.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Vertebral spines from T7 to the sacrum, the posterior third of the iliac crest, the lower three or four ribs and sometimes the inferior angle of the scapula, to the floor of the intertubercular groove. **The scapular slip is scored because Gest scores it as variable**, and it is the interesting one — a muscle of the body wall picking up an attachment on the girdle bone it passes. The origin has spread much further caudally than in any outgroup here; the insertion has not moved, which is the pattern this record shows throughout.

observations.name: Levator scapulae
observations.action: Elevates the scapula.
observations.innervation: Dorsal scapular nerve (C5), with branches from C3 and C4 to the upper part.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Transverse processes of C1-C4 to the medial scapular border between the superior angle and the spine. The double nerve supply is the interesting part and Gest records it: the dorsal scapular nerve to the muscle proper, with direct C3 and C4 branches to its upper part — a segmental gradient surviving inside a muscle that looks unitary.

observations.name: Pectoralis major and minor
observations.action: Major flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm; minor draws the scapula forward and downward.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Major from the medial half of the clavicle, the manubrium and body of the sternum and the costal cartilages of ribs 2-6, occasionally from the rectus sheath, to the crest of the greater tubercle — the human name for the ridge this dataset calls the deltopectoral crest. **Pectoralis minor is scored as the second part of this group rather than as a costocoracoideus**, and the reason is its nerve: it is supplied by the medial pectoral nerve with the rest of the pectoral mass, whereas the reptilian costocoracoideus is a different muscle with a different supply. Its insertion is the striking one — it has left the humerus altogether for the coracoid process, so a limb muscle has become a girdle muscle within the same mass.

observations.name: Rhomboideus major and minor
observations.action: Retracts, elevates and inferiorly rotates the scapula.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Minor from the inferior ligamentum nuchae and the spines of C7-T1 to the medial border at the root of the scapular spine; major from the spines of T2-T5 to the medial border below it. **The record's name is quoted because its deep homology is not established** — Abdala & Diogo single out the 'rhomboideus' and the 'palmaris longus' as the two muscles whose correspondence with the mammalian muscles of those names is under-supported, and this row is the mammalian end of that open question, not evidence for it.

observations.name: Serratus anterior
observations.action: Protracts the scapula; the inferior fibres rotate it superiorly.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Ribs 1-8 or 9 to the costal surface of the medial scapular border — the plesiomorphic arrangement essentially unchanged, which is why this row is worth having as the baseline rather than for anything it reveals. **Two human muscles carry this name and are not this muscle**: serratus posterior superior and inferior run from the vertebral spines to the ribs, are supplied by intercostal nerves, and belong to the body wall, not to the girdle series. They are deliberately not scored here. The name is the only thing they share.

observations.name: Subclavius
observations.action: Draws the clavicle, and with it the shoulder, downward and forward.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). First rib and its cartilage to the inferior surface of the clavicle. **Scored on this record on a correspondence the record itself calls uncertain**: Howell (1937b) derives the subclavius from the sternocoracoideus and Diogo et al. (2009a) review it, but Mivart (1869) made it part of the amphibian procoracohumeralis instead, and the distribution — present in lepidosaurs, birds and monotremes, absent or disputed in turtles, crocodylians and amphibians — does not exclude independent acquisition. The human row is one end of that argument and settles none of it.

observations.name: Subscapularis
observations.action: Medially rotates the arm; assists extension.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medial two-thirds of the costal surface of the scapula to the lesser tubercle. **The human condition is the group with one of its two parts gone**: therians have no coracoid, so the subcoracoideus half of this record has nothing to arise from and the muscle is a subscapularis only. Compare the *Tawa* row on this record, where the two are separate bellies sharing one insertion tendon, and the crocodylian condition, where they are fused but both present.

observations.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus
observations.action: Supraspinatus initiates abduction of the arm; infraspinatus laterally rotates it.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Two fossae either side of the scapular spine to two facets on the greater tubercle, both on the suprascapular nerve. **That shared innervation is the entire argument for the supracoracoideus → supraspinatus + infraspinatus transformation**, and this row is what the argument is about — the scapular spine that divides them is a therian novelty, so the two fossae did not exist to be divided in any outgroup. Gambaryan et al. (2015) attack the transformation from the monotremes, where a supracoracoideus and a supraspinatus and an infraspinatus are all three present at once. Read this row against the monotreme rows on this record, not on its own.

observations.name: Teres major
observations.action: Adducts, medially rotates and assists extension of the arm.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Dorsal surface of the inferior angle of the scapula to the crest of the lesser tubercle, next to the latissimus. That adjacency is the point: this record's assessment reads the muscle's scattered distribution — present in turtles, crocodylians and mammals, absent in amphibians and birds — as repeated differentiation out of the latissimus dorsi and subcoracoscapularis field rather than as one ancestral muscle lost three times, and the human arrangement, with the two insertions on adjacent lips of the same groove, is what that hypothesis predicts.

observations.name: Teres minor
observations.action: Laterally rotates the arm.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Upper two-thirds of the lateral scapular border to the lowest facet of the greater tubercle. **Scored here on a correspondence the record calls proposed and unresolved**, and there are at least four positions on it: the scapulohumeralis anterior → teres minor equation used here; Romer's (1924) derivation of teres minor from the procoracohumeralis instead; Gambaryan et al.'s (2015) reading of the two as sister subdivisions of one reptilian muscle rather than one being the other; and their further suggestion that the acromiodeltoideus is a third portion of the same mass. The axillary nerve this row carries is what the deltoid group and teres minor share, and is the reason the question is live at all.

observations.name: Trapezius and sternocleidomastoid
observations.action: Trapezius elevates, depresses, retracts and superiorly rotates the scapula; sternocleidomastoid flexes and rotates the head.
observations.innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (XI), with proprioceptive fibres from C3-C4.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The clearest single row for what this record is**: the human cucullaris has split in two and the two halves look nothing alike, but both are still innervated by the spinal accessory nerve, which is the criterion the whole homology rests on. The trapezius keeps the ancestral head-to-girdle course; the sternocleidomastoid has reversed it, taking a new origin on the sternum and clavicle and inserting on the skull, so that a girdle protractor became a head rotator without changing its nerve. Gest gives the trapezius insertion as the lateral third of the clavicle, the medial acromion and the crest and tubercle of the scapular spine — three named sites on what is one continuous line in a lizard. The sternocleidomastoid insertion is scored on the occiput because the mastoid process is not a separate element here.

observations.name: Coccygeus
observations.action: Supports the pelvic viscera; draws the coccyx forward.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Ischial spine to the lateral coccyx and the lowest sacrum — the ischiococcygeus under its clinical name. With [[iliocaudalis]] it is the second half of the answer to what happened to the caudal musculature in an animal with no tail: it did not disappear, it took over the pelvic outlet.

observations.name: Gluteus maximus
observations.action: Extends and laterally rotates the thigh.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Posterior gluteal line, the posterior sacrum and coccyx and the sacrotuberous ligament; upper fibres to the iliotibial tract, lowermost to the gluteal tuberosity. **The human muscle is what this record is for**, and its name is one of the clearest false friends in Diogo & Molnar's list: the anuran literature applies 'gluteus maximus' to a muscle that is not this one. It is a mammalian differentiation out of the dorsal iliac field, not an inherited muscle, which is why the record has no reptile or bird rows to compare it against.

observations.name: Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
observations.action: Abduct the thigh and stabilise the pelvis over the stance limb.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medius from the external ilium between the posterior and anterior gluteal lines, minimus between the anterior and inferior lines, both onto the greater trochanter. **This record's whole point is visible here**: the transformation from a modest abductor in a sprawling limb to the principal pelvic stabiliser in a parasagittal one happens with no change of identity, origin, insertion or nerve — the same bone, the same trochanter, the same superior gluteal supply, doing a different job because the limb is held differently. Tensor fasciae latae is scored as a disputed part: it shares the superior gluteal nerve with the other two, but its insertion on the iliotibial tract puts it as easily in the iliotibialis field, and this dataset does not resolve that.

observations.name: Iliococcygeus
observations.action: Supports the pelvic viscera; draws the coccyx forward.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The human pelvic floor is tail musculature that stayed behind.** Iliococcygeus is one of the three parts of levator ani, running from the tendinous arch over the obturator internus fascia to the coccyx and the anococcygeal body. In a lizard the same muscle moves the tail; in an animal whose tail is a coccyx it has become a sling supporting the viscera, without changing either attachment in kind. Gest also lists pubococcygeus, puborectalis, pubovaginalis and levator prostatae, which are the pubic-origin members of the same sheet.

observations.name: Iliopsoas
observations.action: Flexes the thigh at the hip; psoas major also flexes the trunk.
observations.innervation: Femoral nerve, and direct branches of the ventral rami of L1-L4.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Iliacus from the iliac fossa, iliac crest and ala of the sacrum; psoas major from the bodies and transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae; the two join in one tendon onto the lesser trochanter. **The lumbar origin is the change.** In a lizard this muscle is a pelvic muscle taking origin inside the pelvic canal; in a human a whole half of it has climbed onto the vertebral column, which is what lets it flex the trunk as well as the thigh. Psoas minor is scored as a third part and ends on the pelvis rather than the femur — a limb muscle that stopped short of the limb.

observations.name: Obturator externus, quadratus femoris and the gemelli
observations.action: Laterally rotate the thigh; obturator externus also adducts it.
observations.innervation: Obturator nerve to obturator externus; nerve to quadratus femoris and nerve to obturator internus to the remainder.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Obturator externus from the external surface of the obturator membrane and both pubic rami to the trochanteric fossa; quadratus femoris from the lateral ischial tuberosity to the quadrate line; the two gemelli from the ischial spine and tuberosity onto the obturator internus tendon. **Three of the four names here are on Diogo & Molnar's list of false friends** — 'obturator externus', 'quadratus femoris' and 'gemellus' are all applied to non-homologous muscles in the anuran literature. The gemelli are the oddity: they do not reach the femur at all, inserting instead on another muscle's tendon.

observations.name: Piriformis
observations.action: Laterally rotates the extended thigh; abducts the flexed thigh.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Anterior surface of the sacrum to the upper border of the greater trochanter. **Scored on a proposed correspondence, and the proposal is about a lost tail.** This record tracks the fourth trochanter, which is what makes it the most reliably reconstructed hindlimb muscle in fossils; the human femur has no fourth trochanter and the human tail is a coccyx, so what survives is a short sacrum-to-trochanter muscle that has kept the topology and lost the lever. Birds and anurans reduced the same muscle independently, for the same reason.

observations.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **Absent, and the note is about the muscle it is not.** The classical equation makes the amniote 'ambiens' the mammalian sartorius, and Diogo & Molnar reject it: the diagnostic is that the 'ambiens' is a DORSAL muscle sitting in a ventral position, which the sartorius is not. Gest's sartorius runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial tibia through the pes anserinus, on the femoral nerve, and this dataset gives it no home rather than give it a wrong one. The same rejection is why 'tensor fasciae latae' appears on Diogo & Molnar's list of false-friend names.

observations.name: Adductor magnus, longus, brevis and minimus
observations.action: Adduct the thigh; the ischiocondylar part of adductor magnus extends it.
observations.innervation: Obturator nerve, both divisions; the ischiocondylar part of adductor magnus by the tibial nerve, and pectineus by the femoral nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Four adductors from the pubic rami and the ischial tuberosity onto the linea aspera, plus pectineus from the pecten of the pubis to the pectineal line. **The nerve supply is split three ways across one mass** and each split means something: the ischiocondylar part of adductor magnus takes the tibial nerve because it belongs functionally with the hamstrings, and pectineus takes the femoral nerve — and 'pectineus' is another name on Diogo & Molnar's false-friends list. This record also resolves the first of their two contested amphibian muscles: the 'pubifemoralis' is this, not the 'ambiens' it superficially resembles in dorsal view.

observations.name: Gracilis
observations.action: Adducts the thigh and flexes the knee.
observations.innervation: Anterior division of the obturator nerve.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Pubic symphysis and inferior pubic ramus to the medial surface of the tibia through the pes anserinus. **This is the single most important human row in the hindlimb.** Diogo & Molnar single out the gracilis as the one muscle for which the last common ancestor of tetrapods probably had a directly corresponding individual muscle in the modern human sense — everything else in the human hindlimb is a subdivision or a recombination of something that was not a discrete muscle. If a reader wants one row that shows what a one-to-one homology looks like against a whole limb of composites, it is this one.

observations.name: Hamstrings
observations.action: Extend the thigh and flex the knee.
observations.innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve; the short head of biceps femoris by the common fibular division.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). All three from the ischial tuberosity, with a second head of biceps femoris from the lateral lip of the linea aspera, to the fibular head and the two tibial condyles. **The group derives from this field and the head-by-head correspondences are not settled** — Diogo & Molnar reject the classical claim of Gregory & Camp, Romer and Haines that the mammalian tenuissimus is the caudal head of biceps femoris, and follow Jones in deriving it from a dorsal tail-region muscle instead. The human row is therefore the mammalian outcome of the split, not a key to it. The short head of biceps femoris has a different nerve from the rest of the muscle it is named part of, which is the sort of thing that makes the split hard to read.

observations.name: Obturator internus
observations.action: Laterally rotates the thigh.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Internal surface of the obturator membrane and the margin of the obturator foramen, turning through a right angle around the lesser sciatic notch to the medial greater trochanter. **The obturator internus equation is one half of a pair Diogo & Molnar resolved**: of all the amphibian-to-reptile ventral pelvic homologies they found only two contested, the 'pubifemoralis' and the 'ischiofemoralis', and they resolve the second as this muscle. Note that obturator internus and obturator externus arise from the two faces of the same membrane and belong to different homology groups.

observations.name: Rectus femoris
observations.action: Extends the knee and flexes the hip.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Straight head from the anterior inferior iliac spine, reflected head from above the acetabular rim, to the patella and the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament. **The rectus femoris is why the quadriceps is a composite of two different ancestral muscles**: it comes from this record and the three vasti come from the femorotibialis, which is exactly why the rectus crosses the hip and the vasti do not. Read the two rows together — one human muscle group, two homology groups, and the joint each part spans is the tell. The urodele end of this record is actively disputed: Kardong derives femorotibialis, iliotibialis and 'ambiens' from three separate salamander muscles, Gadow, Walker and Diogo & Molnar from one.

observations.name: Vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius
observations.action: Extend the knee; articularis genu retracts the suprapatellar bursa.
observations.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Three vasti from the anterior, lateral and medial femoral shaft and the two lips of the linea aspera, onto the patella. **One of the least contested correspondences in the hindlimb** — a femur-to-tibia extensor that never crosses the hip, in every tetrapod that has one. Articularis genu is scored as a fourth part: it is a few fibres of vastus intermedius that stop at the knee capsule instead of reaching the patella, and it is the smallest thing in this dataset that still counts as a muscle.

observations.name: Splenius capitis
observations.attachmentNote: **Splenius capitis** (Gest). Nuchal ligament and the spines of the last cervical and upper thoracic vertebrae, forward and upward to the mastoid process and the lateral end of the superior nuchal line. Its fibre direction is why it is worth separating: it runs spine-to-skull, obliquely across the transversospinal sheet beneath it, which runs transverse-process-to-spine. Two layers of one segmental series crossing each other, both on dorsal rami. Gest lists an undivided splenius as well as the capitis and cervicis parts, so the three entries are two insertions of one muscle.

observations.name: Splenius cervicis
observations.attachmentNote: **Splenius cervicis** (Gest). Same origin as the capitis part, ending instead on the posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the first three cervical vertebrae.

observations.name: Obliquus capitis inferior
observations.attachmentNote: **Obliquus capitis inferior** (Gest). Spine of the axis to the transverse process of the atlas — the one suboccipital muscle that never reaches the skull. It rotates the atlas, and the head rides on it.

observations.name: Obliquus capitis superior
observations.attachmentNote: **Obliquus capitis superior** (Gest). Transverse process of the atlas to the occipital bone above the inferior nuchal line.

observations.name: Rectus capitis posterior major
observations.attachmentNote: **Rectus capitis posterior major** (Gest). Spine of the axis to the inferior nuchal line. With the two obliqui it bounds the suboccipital triangle, and all four suboccipital muscles take the dorsal ramus of C1. That is the whole reason the group is epaxial: nothing about where they attach separates them from the prevertebral muscles a centimetre away, and the nerve does.

observations.name: Rectus capitis posterior minor
observations.attachmentNote: **Rectus capitis posterior minor** (Gest). Posterior tubercle of the atlas to the medial part of the inferior nuchal line, deep and medial to the major. The atlas has no spine, which is why the two recti capitis posteriores start on different kinds of thing.

observations.name: Interspinales
observations.attachmentNote: **Interspinales** (Gest). Spine to the spine above, one segment at a time, the whole length of the column. Gest calls them small and mechanically unimportant, and they are; as a homology statement they are the least modified thing in the human back, a segmental muscle still spanning one segment.

observations.name: Intertransversarii
observations.attachmentNote: **Intertransversarii** (Gest). Transverse process to the transverse process above. Gest gives the whole series dorsal rami, which is why it is scored on an epaxial record; the cervical and lumbar members take ventral rami at least in part on most other accounts, and if that is right then some of this muscle is hypaxial and the row lumps two fields. Nothing in this source separates them.

observations.name: Multifidus
observations.attachmentNote: **Multifidus** (Gest). Sacrum and the transverse processes of C3 to L5, up two to four segments onto the spines.

observations.name: Rotatores
observations.attachmentNote: **Rotatores** (Gest). Transverse process to the spine one or two segments above; the shortest fascicles of the series, and the deepest.

observations.name: Semispinalis
observations.attachmentNote: **Semispinalis** (Gest). Transverse processes of C7-T12 to the spines four to six segments above, and, in the capitis part, onto the occipital bone between the nuchal lines. Semispinalis capitis is the only member of this series that ends on the skull, and it is most of the muscle mass behind the neck.

observations.name: Spinalis
observations.attachmentNote: **Spinalis** (Gest). Spines below to spines above, and to the base of the skull. Gest counts it as the medial of the three erector spinae columns and this record is the medial epaxial tract, so it is scored here rather than beside the iliocostalis and longissimus rows — which is how the human row on `epaxial-musculature` already lists it. It runs spine-to-spine, not transverse-process-to-spine, so the record's name misdescribes this member of it.
